title: Network lab: pfSense, Pi-hole and a client
summary: A router (pfSense CE) in front of an isolated LAN where Pi-hole serves DNS and DHCP and a Lubuntu desktop is the user. The exercises read what the three members do for each other; the tests check the same things over SSH.

exercises.title: DNS and DHCP from Pi-hole
exercises.text: Pi-hole is the LAN's DNS and DHCP server: pfSense hands the clients to it and asks it for its own names. Everything here is read-only.

commands: sudo pihole-FTL --config dhcp.active       # true: Pi-hole is the LAN's DHCP server
sudo pihole-FTL --config dhcp.hosts        # the fixed leases of the members
resolvectl status | grep -A3 'Link.*enp'    # DNS 192.168.0.10, domain qlan
resolvectl query example.org                # a public name, answered by Pi-hole through pfSense
sudo pihole -g                              # refresh the blocklists (gravity): a few seconds, nothing else changes

exercises.title: Through the firewall
exercises.text: The client reaches the Internet only through pfSense: its default route is the router's LAN address and the router NATs on its WAN (the slirp network of the host).

commands: curl -sI https://example.org | head -1       # HTTP/2 200 through the pfSense NAT
systemd-analyze                              # the boot time of a client that waits for no network
ifconfig vtnet1 | grep inet                  # the LAN side, 192.168.0.1
netstat -rn | head -5                        # the default route over the WAN
vmctl lab check                              # the five forwards on 127.0.0.1: pfSense GUI 8080, Pi-hole UI 8081, SSH 2237/2238/2239
